title: Phaedo
author: Plato
openingText: Were you yourself, Phaedo, in the prison with Socrates on the day when he drank the poison? I was, Echecrates. What did he say in his last hours? We will tell you, he said, all that occurred. I have always a singular delight in any discourse about philosophy, whether I hear it myself or remember it from others.
about: Socrates is in prison, hours before his execution. His friends are crying. He explains why he is not afraid to die. Then he drinks the hemlock.

angleCards.title: The arguments for immortality.
angleCards.text: Socrates offers four separate arguments that the soul survives death. I want to follow each one carefully — understand where it works, where it fails, and whether any of them actually establish what he claims.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading the Phaedo to evaluate the four arguments for the soul's immortality — I want to understand which is the strongest, which fails, and what Plato actually believes he has proven.

angleCards.title: Performance or conviction?
angleCards.text: Socrates argues brilliantly for immortality while his friends weep. I want to read carefully for signs of whether he genuinely believes his arguments — or whether he is, in his last hours, performing courage for others.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading the Phaedo to understand whether Socrates actually believes what he argues — or whether he is performing courage for his grieving friends, giving them comfort rather than truth.

angleCards.title: Death as a philosophical problem.
angleCards.text: Socrates argues that philosophy is practice for dying — that the philosopher has been separating soul from body all along. I want to understand what this implies about how one should actually live.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading the Phaedo to understand Socrates' argument that a philosopher should welcome death — that philosophy itself is a kind of preparation for dying, and what that means for how one should live.

angleCards.title: The last scene.
angleCards.text: The death of Socrates is one of the most carefully written scenes in all of ancient literature. I want to read it asking what Plato is doing — what he is preserving, what he is constructing, and why he wrote it this way.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading the Phaedo for the last scene — the death of Socrates — and to understand what Plato is doing in writing it with such extraordinary literary care, as the most controlled piece of writing in all of ancient philosophy.

cast.name: Socrates
cast.description: Spends his last hours in philosophical argument rather than farewell. Sends his wife home early because her weeping is not useful. Is more interested in the arguments than in his own death.

cast.name: Phaedo
cast.description: A student of Socrates who was present at the death. Recounts the entire day to Echecrates from memory. His emotional responses — weeping, laughing, wondering — become the reader's guide.

cast.name: Cebes
cast.description: Presses Socrates most rigorously. Raises the objection that even if the soul is immortal, it might wear out through repeated incarnations. The dialogue's sharpest interlocutor.

cast.name: Simmias
cast.description: Raises the harmony argument — the idea that the soul might be like the tuning of a lyre, destroyed when the instrument is. Socrates takes it seriously and spends considerable time answering it.

cast.name: Echecrates
cast.description: The Pythagorean philosopher to whom Phaedo tells the whole story. His questions and reactions give the dialogue its outer frame — we hear the story as he hears it, from someone who was there.

cast.name: The Soul
cast.description: Not a character but the subject — what it is, whether it is immortal, what it does between incarnations. Every argument in the dialogue turns on what kind of thing the soul is and whether that kind of thing can die.
